title: Finding an Idea and Letting It Evolve
goal: The goal this week isn't to learn a song—it's to discover a short musical phrase that could become your piece.

source.description: Complete user-supplied original lesson; publication date verified against earlier conversation record

originalText:
Weekly Keyboard Practice (20–30 minutes)
Theme: Finding an idea and letting it evolve
The goal this week isn't to learn a song—it's to discover a short musical phrase that could become your piece.

1. Black-Key Exploration (5 minutes)
Set a simple metronome or beat-only track around 70–80 BPM.

Using only the black keys, spend a few minutes improvising without worrying about harmony. Since the black keys form a pentatonic scale, almost everything will sound cohesive.

Try:

Short 3–5 note ideas.
Lots of silence between phrases.
Repeating one motif, changing only the rhythm.
Don't chase complexity—look for one phrase you genuinely like.

2. New Chord Voicings (7 minutes)
Keep your right hand improvising on the black keys while your left hand experiments with these simple voicings:

B♭sus2 → (B♭–C–F)
G♭maj7(no3) → (G♭–D♭–F)
D♭add9 → (D♭–E♭–A♭)
Don't think about the names while playing. Listen for:

Which chord feels like "home."
Which chord creates tension.
Which transition surprises you.
Hold each chord for several measures before changing.

3. Split Voice Experiment (5–7 minutes)
On your Roland GO:KEYS 3:

Left: Warm pad or soft strings.
Right: Felt piano or mellow electric piano.
Play sustained chords with the pad while letting the piano speak in short melodic phrases.

Focus on dynamics:

Let the pad stay almost motionless.
Allow the piano to become the storyteller.
4. Build Your Own Piece (8–10 minutes)
Keep the beat-only track running.

Challenge yourself to create:

An A section (about 20–30 seconds).
Repeat it.
Change only one thing:
rhythm,
ending,
bass note,
or one chord.
That's the beginning of a B section.

Record the whole improvisation on your keyboard or phone. Don't stop if you make mistakes—sometimes the best ideas happen when you're trying to recover.

Listening Inspiration (Apple Music)
Retrograde — James Blake
Listen for:

Space between phrases.
Minimal harmony.
How repetition slowly evolves into something emotional.
The way texture changes without becoming busy.
Experience — Ludovico Einaudi
Listen for:

Building intensity through repetition rather than complexity.
Small harmonic shifts creating a large emotional impact.
The patience of the arrangement—nothing feels rushed.
This week's creative challenge
By the end of the session, try to have one 20–30 second idea that you would actually want to hear again tomorrow. Don't judge whether it's "finished." Your only goal is to capture a musical seed worth revisiting.

title: Movement Through Suspended Harmony
goal: This week, focus on creating music that feels like it's always moving forward without needing a dramatic melody. Think shimmering, suspended, and patient.

source.description: Complete user-supplied original lesson; publication date verified against earlier conversation record

originalText:
Weekly Keyboard Practice (20–30 minutes)
Theme: Movement Through Suspended Harmony
This week, focus on creating music that feels like it's always moving forward without needing a dramatic melody. Think shimmering, suspended, and patient.

1. Black-Key Exploration (5 minutes)
Set a beat-only track between 78–88 BPM.

Stay entirely on the black keys. Instead of running up and down the scale, limit yourself to four notes for the first few minutes.

Try this idea:

Play a short motif.
Repeat it three times.
On the fourth repetition, change only one note.
Amazing ideas often come from tiny changes rather than brand-new phrases.

2. Chord Voicing Exploration (7 minutes)
This week, experiment with open voicings that leave lots of space.

Try these left-hand shapes:

D♭maj9 (no 3rd) → D♭ – A♭ – E♭
A♭add9 → A♭ – E♭ – B♭
G♭maj7 → G♭ – D♭ – F
Hold each chord while your right hand improvises only on the black keys.

Notice how changing the bass note underneath the same melody completely changes the emotional color.

3. Split/Dual Voice Experiment (6 minutes)
On your Roland GO:KEYS 3:

Left hand: Warm analog pad or soft synth strings.
Right hand: Electric piano or a mellow bell/felt piano layer.
Keep the pad sustaining underneath while your right hand plays lightly. Aim for contrast: broad, slow harmony below and delicate movement above.

If your keyboard supports it, add just a touch of reverb to let notes bloom into each other.

4. Build Your Own Piece (10 minutes)
Continue over the beat-only track.

Structure your improvisation like this:

30 seconds: Introduce one motif.
30 seconds: Repeat it with a different chord underneath.
30 seconds: Strip it back to almost nothing.
30 seconds: Bring the full texture back with both hands.
Record the session. Afterwards, listen back once and identify one moment that made you stop and think, "I'd like to hear that again." That's your starting point for your next original piece.

Listening Inspiration (Apple Music)
Glue — Bicep
Listen for:

The hypnotic repetition.
How tiny harmonic and textural changes keep the track evolving.
The way space is used between layers instead of filling every moment.
Skulls — Röyksopp
Listen for:

Shimmering analog synth textures.
Wide, suspended harmonies that feel cinematic.
How the arrangement gradually unfolds without relying on flashy solos.
Creative Challenge
Before you finish, give your new idea a working title—even if it's something simple like "Rain on Glass," "Late Drive," or "Static Bloom." Naming an idea helps your brain treat it as something worth returning to, rather than just another improvisation.

title: Layers That Breathe
goal: This week, focus on making your music feel wide and cinematic without adding lots of notes. The exercise is about restraint—letting harmony, texture, and timing create interest.

source.description: Complete user-supplied original lesson; publication date verified against earlier conversation record

originalText:
Weekly Keyboard Practice (20–30 minutes)
Theme: Layers That Breathe
This week, focus on making your music feel wide and cinematic without adding lots of notes. The exercise is about restraint—letting harmony, texture, and timing create interest.

1. Black-Key Exploration (5 minutes)
Start a beat-only track around 82–90 BPM.

For the first five minutes, stay entirely on the black keys.

Rules:

Play only 2–4 notes at a time.
Leave at least one measure of silence after every phrase.
Repeat each idea before changing it.
Listen for which motifs naturally invite a chord underneath.

2. Chord Voicing Study (7 minutes)
This week, explore quartal-inspired (stacked fourths) and suspended sounds.

Try these left-hand shapes:

E♭ – A♭ – D♭
B♭ – E♭ – A♭
D♭ – G♭ – B♭
Don't worry about naming every chord. Instead, notice how they create openness and avoid sounding overly "major" or "minor."

While holding each voicing, improvise gently on the black keys with your right hand.

3. Split/Dual Voice Exercise (6 minutes)
On your Roland GO:KEYS 3:

Left hand: Warm synth pad or soft strings.
Right hand: Felt piano layered lightly with a bell or airy synth.
Try this approach:

Sustain a chord for four measures.
Play a simple melody.
Instead of changing the melody, change only the underlying chord.
Observe how the emotional character shifts even though the notes stay similar.
4. Develop an Original Idea (8–10 minutes)
Keep the beat running.

Create a one-minute sketch using this structure:

0:00–0:20 — Introduce a motif.
0:20–0:40 — Repeat it with a new bass note or voicing.
0:40–1:00 — Strip it back to almost nothing, then end with a sustained chord.
Record the entire take. When you listen back, don't evaluate the performance—identify the single phrase that has the strongest emotional pull. That's the idea worth developing next week.

Listening Inspiration (Apple Music)
A Walk — Tycho
Listen for:

The gradual layering of sounds.
How repetition creates momentum instead of monotony.
The balance between rhythmic pulse and spacious harmony.
Sherbrooke — Thylacine
Listen for:

Evolving textures that never feel crowded.
Subtle harmonic movement over a steady groove.
How small changes in timbre and rhythm keep the music engaging.
Creative Challenge
Before you finish, choose one chord voicing from today's session that surprised you. Build your next original piece around that harmony instead of starting with a melody. Often, an unusual harmonic color is what gives a piece its unique identity.

title: Tension, Release, and Long Lines
goal: This week is about making music that feels like it's going somewhere. Instead of thinking in individual notes, think in phrases that slowly unfold over several measures.

source.description: Complete user-supplied original lesson; publication date verified against earlier conversation record

originalText:
Weekly Keyboard Practice (20–30 minutes)
Theme: Tension, Release, and Long Lines
This week is about making music that feels like it's going somewhere. Instead of thinking in individual notes, think in phrases that slowly unfold over several measures.

1. Black-Key Exploration (5 minutes)
Choose a beat-only track around 72–84 BPM.

Stay entirely on the black keys.

For the first few minutes, use this rule:

Play one short phrase (3–6 notes).
Wait two beats.
Answer it with a different phrase.
Repeat that "conversation" several times before inventing something new.
Imagine you're writing a melody that someone could hum.

2. Chord Voicing Discovery (7 minutes)
This week, explore major 9 and add9 colors that feel spacious without sounding overly jazzy.

Try these left-hand voicings:

G♭maj9 (open) → G♭ – D♭ – F – A♭
D♭add9 → D♭ – A♭ – E♭
A♭6/9 → A♭ – E♭ – F – B♭
Don't worry about perfect theory. Listen for how each chord changes the emotional weight of the exact same melody.

As an experiment, keep your right hand playing the same melodic idea while changing only the left-hand chord.

3. Split/Dual Voice Texture (6 minutes)
On your Roland GO:KEYS 3:

Left hand: Soft analog pad or warm strings.
Right hand: Felt piano layered quietly with a glassy synth or soft EP.
Begin with just the pad for four measures.

Then fade the piano in naturally.

Rather than playing louder, make the arrangement feel bigger simply by adding another layer.

4. Build an Original Sketch (8–10 minutes)
Keep the beat running.

Create a simple two-part structure:

Part A (30 seconds)

Sparse melody.
One or two chords.
Lots of breathing room.
Part B (30 seconds)

Same motif.
New bass movement.
Slightly fuller texture.
Then return to Part A, but play it more quietly than when you started.

Record the entire minute and don't stop for mistakes. You're collecting ideas, not performing.

Listening Inspiration (Apple Music)
On the Nature of Daylight — Max Richter
Listen for:

Long, singing melodic lines.
How repetition becomes more emotional through subtle harmonic movement.
The gradual expansion of texture without increasing complexity.
La Perla — Sofiane Pamart
Listen for:

Spacious piano voicings.
The balance between rhythm and silence.
How a simple motif evolves through touch and dynamics rather than fast playing.
Creative Challenge
Spend the last two minutes with your eyes closed.

Don't think about scales or chords. Instead, imagine you're scoring the opening scene of a film: dawn over an empty city, fog lifting from a valley, or headlights on a quiet highway.

When you're finished, save the recording with today's date. If there's even one 10-second passage that makes you want to hear it again tomorrow, you've succeeded. Over time, those small fragments become the raw material for complete original pieces.

title: Warm R&B / Late-Night Groove
goal: Goal: get one smooth 4-chord loop into your hands, then stop “practicing” it and start making it your own.

source.description: Complete user-supplied original lesson; publication date verified against earlier conversation record

originalText:
This week: Warm R&B / late-night groove
Time: about 25 minutes
Goal: get one smooth 4-chord loop into your hands, then stop “practicing” it and start making it your own.
1. Black-key warm-up — 4 minutes
Use only these right-hand notes:

D♭ – E♭ – G♭ – A♭ – B♭

Start with this little phrase:

RH: A♭ → B♭ → G♭ → E♭

Then answer it with:

RH: G♭ → E♭ → D♭

Play slowly. Leave space between the two phrases. After a minute or two, forget my pattern and just wander around those five notes.

Your only job: when you accidentally play something you like, repeat it.
2. Your main 4-chord loop — 7 minutes
Play these in order.

1. LH: D♭ + A♭ | RH: D♭ + F + A♭

2. LH: B♭ + F | RH: D♭ + F + A♭

3. LH: G♭ + D♭ | RH: D♭ + F + B♭

4. LH: A♭ + E♭ | RH: C + E♭ + A♭

Then go straight back to #1.

Notice something important: from chord 1 to chord 2, your right hand doesn't move at all. Only the left hand changes.

For the first few minutes, don't add rhythm. Press both hands together and hold each chord for four counts:

1 – 2 – 3 – 4

Change on the next 1.

Keep looping until you no longer have to hunt for every note.
3. Give it a groove — 5 minutes
Now count:

1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &

For every chord:

1: press BOTH hands
2: keep holding
3: lift and replay the RIGHT hand only
4: let everything ring

Think:

BOTH — hold — RH — hold

Then move to the next chord on the next 1.

Don't try to make it fancy yet. The slight right-hand hit on beat 3 is enough to turn the progression from “four chords” into something that starts feeling like music.
One optional variation
Once the basic rhythm feels automatic, move that second RH hit from 3 to the & after 2:

1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &
BOTH — — RH — — — —

That little early hit creates much more of an R&B pocket.
4. Put it over a beat — 7–8 minutes
Find a beat-only track around 76–84 BPM.

For the first couple minutes, simply play the four-chord loop exactly as above.

Then simplify the left hand to one note:

LH: D♭ | RH: D♭ + F + A♭
LH: B♭ | RH: D♭ + F + A♭
LH: G♭ | RH: D♭ + F + B♭
LH: A♭ | RH: C + E♭ + A♭

Once that feels secure, occasionally skip the RH chord and use your black-key notes instead:

D♭ – E♭ – G♭ – A♭ – B♭

Don't try to solo continuously. Play a few notes, then leave space while the beat continues.

That's where I want the lesson to turn into your music.
5. Optional GO:KEYS 3 sound experiment — 3 minutes
The GO:KEYS 3 supports both Split and Dual, so use Split this week: low keyboard for one sound, upper keyboard for another. Roland lists more than 1,100 ZEN-Core tones on the instrument. Roland

Keep it simple:

Left: choose a soft synth-bass tone.
Right: choose an electric-piano tone.

You don't need a pad this week—the bass + EP combination makes it much easier to hear exactly what each hand is contributing.

Keep the LH extremely simple:

D♭ → B♭ → G♭ → A♭

Let the electric piano handle the chords and little melodic answers above it.
🎧 Listen for the feeling
“Damage” — H.E.R. is on Apple Music. Apple Music - Web Player

Don't try to copy the song. Listen specifically to how the keyboard harmony sits behind the groove instead of constantly demanding attention. The chords feel relaxed because there's room around them.

For a more electronic interpretation of the same lesson, try “A Walk” — Tycho, also on Apple Music. Apple Music - Web Player Listen for how a relatively simple repeating idea becomes interesting through pulse, layering, and gradual changes, rather than lots of new notes. Apple Music describes Dive as pairing arpeggiated keys and atmospheric textures with a strong bass foundation, which is very close to what you're experimenting with here. Apple Music - Web Player
What I want you to get out of this one
By the end, you should be able to turn on a beat and play:

D♭ → B♭ → G♭ → A♭

without needing to stop and calculate what comes next.

Once your hands know the loop, that's when the actual musical exploration starts.

RH: D♭ – E♭ – G♭ – A♭ – B♭

RH: A♭ → G♭ → E♭ → D♭

Then:

RH: E♭ → G♭ → A♭

③ LH: D♭ + A♭ | RH: D♭ + F + A♭

1 – 2 – 3 – 4

1: press LH + RH together
2: keep holding
3: release RH and press it again
4: hold

Your left hand stays down the whole measure.

RH: PRESS ─── PRESS ─── HOLD

Then change everything together on the next 1.

LH: G♭ + D♭ | RH: D♭ + F + B♭

Dual tone: Soft Warm Pad

When you play:

E♭ → G♭ → D♭

don't immediately ask yourself “what do I play next?”

Stay there.

Play it again.

Change the melody slightly.

Leave more silence.

Play it an octave higher.

title: Melodic House / Electronic Pulse
goal: This week is about getting a repeating pattern into your fingers so the keyboard starts sounding like a synth part rather than a piano playing block chords.

source.description: Complete user-supplied original lesson; publication date verified against earlier conversation record

originalText:
Weekly Keyboard Practice


This week: Melodic house / electronic pulse
Time: ~25 minutes. This week is about getting a repeating pattern into your fingers so the keyboard starts sounding like a synth part rather than a piano playing block chords.

1. Five-note warm-up — 3 minutes
Use only these right-hand notes:

F – A♭ – B♭ – C – E♭

Play:

RH: F → A♭ → B♭ → C → E♭ → C → B♭ → A♭

Then:

RH: C → B♭ → A♭ → F

Repeat slowly. After a minute, stop following my exact order and make little 3–5 note phrases using only those five notes.

Leave gaps. A short phrase followed by silence will sound much more musical than constantly filling every beat.

2. Learn these four shapes — 6 minutes
Don't worry about their chord names. Learn where your hands go.

① LH: F + C | RH: A♭ + C + E♭
② LH: D♭ + A♭ | RH: A♭ + D♭ + F
③ LH: A♭ + E♭ | RH: A♭ + C + E♭
④ LH: E♭ + B♭ | RH: G + B♭ + E♭

Then back to ①.

At first, press both hands together:

1 – 2 – 3 – 4

Press on 1, hold through 4, release just before the next 1.

Do that until you can move through all four without stopping.

3. Turn the chords into a synth pattern — 5 minutes
Now we're going to arpeggiate them. Arpeggiate simply means playing the notes of a chord one at a time instead of all together.

For every chord, your LH holds while your RH cycles through its three notes.

Count:

1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &

For chord ①:

LH: F + C — press on 1 and HOLD the entire measure.
RH: A♭ → C → E♭ → C → A♭ → C → E♭ → C

Match the notes exactly to the count:

Count: 1 | & | 2 | & | 3 | & | 4 | &
RH: A♭ | C | E♭ | C | A♭ | C | E♭ | C

Play each RH note separately. Release it as you move to the next one.

Then use exactly the same low → middle → high → middle movement for the other chords:

② LH: D♭ + A♭ | RH: A♭ → D♭ → F → D♭ → A♭ → D♭ → F → D♭

③ LH: A♭ + E♭ | RH: A♭ → C → E♭ → C → A♭ → C → E♭ → C

④ LH: E♭ + B♭ | RH: G → B♭ → E♭ → B♭ → G → B♭ → E♭ → B♭

One measure each. Then repeat.

Don't speed it up until the RH motion starts feeling almost mindless.

4. Put drums underneath it — 8 minutes
Aim for about 108–112 BPM.

You can actually do this entirely on the GO:KEYS 3: start a Style whose drums you like, then use Part Mute to remove the bass and backing parts so you're essentially left with the rhythm section. Roland specifically supports muting accompaniment parts and lists separate drums, bass, and backing elements. 

For the first 4 minutes, play exactly what you learned:

LH: F + C | RH: A♭ → C → E♭ → C…
LH: D♭ + A♭ | RH: A♭ → D♭ → F → D♭…
LH: A♭ + E♭ | RH: A♭ → C → E♭ → C…
LH: E♭ + B♭ | RH: G → B♭ → E♭ → B♭…

Keep the drums going and loop it.

For the last 4 minutes, stop the repeating RH pattern.

Play only one LH note at the beginning of each measure:

LH: F → D♭ → A♭ → E♭

Now use your five warm-up notes for the RH:

RH: F – A♭ – B♭ – C – E♭

Try a tiny phrase, wait, then answer it.

If you stumble onto something that sounds good, repeat it for several loops instead of immediately inventing something new. That's how the exercise starts turning into an actual song idea.

5. Optional GO:KEYS 3 sound experiment — 3 minutes
Try Dual this week.

Main tone: Heartbeat Pluck
Dual tone: Soft Warm Pad

Those are both actual factory tones on the GO:KEYS 3: Heartbeat Pluck is in Synth Pluck, and Soft Warm Pad is in Synth Pad/Str. 

That combination should suit this exercise really well: the pluck makes every individual RH note obvious, while the pad leaves a soft tail underneath it.

Try the repeating pattern again:

LH: F + C | RH: A♭ → C → E♭ → C…

With the new sound, you'll probably hear why electronic keyboard parts so often use individual repeating notes instead of full chord hits.

🎧 Listen for this
I checked Apple Music; both of these are available there.

Disclosure — “Latch (feat. Sam Smith)”
Don't worry about learning its actual chords. Listen for the short synth/keyboard sounds and the rhythmic spaces between them. Notice how little attacks can create movement without a pianist hammering full chords constantly.

RÜFÜS DU SOL — “Innerbloom (Radio Edit)”
Listen for something different: repetition. A musical idea can stay around for a long time while the arrangement slowly changes around it. That's exactly the habit I want you experimenting with today.

The thing to get comfortable with today
By the end, I want this physical motion to feel natural:

LH holds → RH low / middle / high / middle → repeat

You don't need another chord progression, scale, or technique today. If that one movement starts feeling automatic over a beat, you've got plenty to play with.

title: Week 7 — Brazilian-Inspired Pop
goal: Today's goal: Learn four smooth hand shapes, then make them dance around each other.

source.description: Complete user-supplied original lesson; publication date verified against earlier conversation record

originalText:
🎹 Week 7 — Brazilian-Inspired Pop
A little bossa nova, a little jazz, and a relaxed summer-evening groove
Time: 25 minutes | Tempo: 80 BPM | Difficulty: Easy–Intermediate

This week we're changing direction. Instead of the driving rhythms of disco or electronic music, we're going for something lighter, almost like a conversation between your hands.

Bossa nova is a Brazilian musical style with a gentle, swaying rhythm. The interesting part is that the low notes and higher chords don't always land together.

Today's goal: Learn four smooth hand shapes, then make them dance around each other.

① Warm-up — 3 minutes
Five notes, one hand, no pressure.

Start somewhere around the middle of your keyboard.

LH: — | RH: C → D → E → G → A

Come back down:

LH: — | RH: A → G → E → D → C

Now play this little melody:

LH: — | RH: E → G → A → G → E

Pause.

LH: — | RH: D → E → C

Play these slowly. Don't count yet.

After a minute, experiment with those five notes. Make up little phrases and repeat anything you like.

Listen for: Which notes sound like they're asking a question? Which ones sound like they've finished a sentence?

② Four chords — 6 minutes
We're using four slightly richer sounds than we've played in some previous weeks. A couple of extra notes give them that warm, sophisticated feel.

Play them in this exact order.

①
LH: A + E | RH: G + C + E

②
LH: D + A | RH: F + A + C

③
LH: G + D | RH: F + B + D

④
LH: C + G | RH: E + G + B

Repeat: ① → ② → ③ → ④

For now, forget rhythm.

Press both hands together on 1.

Count 1 – 2 – 3 – 4, holding everything down.

Release just before the next 1, then move to the next shape.

Notice how the right-hand notes don't move very far between chords. That's intentional.

Spend the full six minutes just getting these four shapes comfortable.

③ The rhythm — 5 minutes
Here's where things get interesting.

Previously, we've played chords directly on the numbered beats. Today your right hand will occasionally play between them.

That's called syncopation: emphasizing a moment between the main beats.

Count out loud
1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &

Think of the numbers as your footsteps and the & as the moments between them.

Here's the pattern:

Count	1	&	2	&	3	&	4	&
LH	●	—	—	—	●	—	—	—
RH	—	—	—	●	—	—	●	—
● = Press the notes.

For chord ①:

LH: A + E | RH: G + C + E

Follow these exact instructions:

1: Press LH. Release on the following &.
& after 2: Press RH. Release on 3.
3: Press LH again. Release on the following &.
4: Press RH again. Release on the following &.
Then move to chord ② and repeat.

Every note should be fairly short, but don't make it aggressive.

You're going for:

BOOM ... cha ... BOOM ... cha

Except that first little cha arrives slightly later than you might expect.

Once this clicks, you'll hear that relaxed Brazilian-inspired sway.

④ Over a drum track — 8 minutes
Let's actually make music.

Try this 80 BPM drum-only backing track on YouTube. It's a general groove rather than a dedicated bossa rhythm, but it's slow enough to work with today's pattern. 

First 3 minutes: Just play
Keep cycling through:

① LH: A + E | RH: G + C + E
② LH: D + A | RH: F + A + C
③ LH: G + D | RH: F + B + D
④ LH: C + G | RH: E + G + B

One full count of 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & for each chord.

Don't stop if you miss something. Get back into the groove.

Next 5 minutes: Make it yours
Keep the same four-chord loop, but occasionally replace a right-hand chord with a little melody.

Use only:

C – D – E – G – A

Here's something to try:

LH: A + E | RH: E → G → A

Then return to your usual chord playing.

LH: D + A | RH: F + A + C

Play a little more.

LH: G + D | RH: D → E → G

Then:

LH: C + G | RH: E + G + B

Don't worry about fitting every melody note perfectly into the rhythm yet.

Play a phrase, listen to the drums, and answer yourself.

Try to find one short melody that you genuinely enjoy hearing repeated.

⑤ Optional: GO:KEYS 3 sound experiment — 3 minutes
Let's make your keyboard sound like two different musicians.

This week, use Split.

Split means the lower and upper areas of your keyboard play different instrument sounds.

Set up your sounds
LOWER: Acoustic Bass
UPPER: Nylon Gtr 1

Both are actual factory tones on the Roland GO:KEYS 3, in the acoustic bass and acoustic guitar categories. 

To activate them:

Press [split/dual] until the display shows Split.
Select LOWER using [f1] and choose Acoustic Bass.
Select UPPER using [f2] and choose Nylon Gtr 1.
These controls follow Roland's GO:KEYS 3 reference instructions. 

One optional variation

title: Week 8 — Retro Funk & Soul
goal: Today's goal: Get three chord shapes comfortable, learn one funky rhythm, and spend eight minutes making your own groove.

originalText:
🎹 Week 8 — Retro Funk & Soul
Think Stevie Wonder meets modern funky keyboard grooves.
Time: 25 minutes | Tempo: 95 BPM | Difficulty: Easy–Intermediate

This week we're going for something a little dirtier, funkier, and more playful.

Last week you practiced making your hands move independently with a relaxed Brazilian rhythm. Today we're keeping that independence but making everything short, punchy, and rhythmic.

The secret to funk is often what you don't play.

Today's goal: Get three chord shapes comfortable, learn one funky rhythm, and spend eight minutes making your own groove.

① Warm-up — 3 minutes
Five notes, a little attitude
Start around the middle of your keyboard.

LH: — | RH: C → E♭ → F → G → B♭

Come back down:

LH: — | RH: B♭ → G → F → E♭ → C

Now play this little phrase:

LH: — | RH: C → E♭ → F

Pause.

LH: — | RH: G → F → E♭ → C

Repeat it a few times.

Then start changing the rhythm. Make some notes short, others longer.

Don't worry about timing yet. Just get comfortable with those five notes.

② Your three chord shapes — 6 minutes
We're using three warm, slightly bluesy sounds.

Play them in this order:

①
LH: F + C | RH: A♭ + C + E♭

②
LH: B♭ + F | RH: A♭ + D + F

③
LH: C + G | RH: B♭ + E♭ + G

④ Back to shape ②
LH: B♭ + F | RH: A♭ + D + F

Then repeat from ①.

Your complete loop: ① → ② → ③ → ②

First, play them slowly.
Count:

1 – 2 – 3 – 4

Press both hands together on 1.

Hold everything through 2, 3, 4.

Release just before the next 1, then change chords.

Keep repeating until your fingers start remembering where to go.

Notice the darker sound of chord ① compared with the brighter chord ②.

③ Learn the funk rhythm — 5 minutes
This is today's main exercise.

We're going to make the left hand sound like a bass player and the right hand sound like a funky rhythm guitarist.

Count out loud:

1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &

Count	1	&	2	&	3	&	4	&
LH	●	—	—	—	●	—	—	—
RH	—	●	—	—	—	●	—	—
● = Press. A dash means don't press anything new.

Here's exactly what to do for chord ①:

LH: F + C | RH: A♭ + C + E♭

1: Press LH.
& after 1: Release LH and press RH.
2: Release RH.
& after 2: Silence.
3: Press LH again.
& after 3: Release LH and press RH.
4: Release RH.
& after 4: Silence.

Then change to chord ② on the next 1.

The silence is important!

Don't hold the notes. Each hit should be short.

Think:

BASS-chuck ... BASS-chuck ...

This is a form of syncopation, which simply means placing musical accents between the main numbered beats.

Practice the whole loop
① LH: F + C | RH: A♭ + C + E♭
② LH: B♭ + F | RH: A♭ + D + F
③ LH: C + G | RH: B♭ + E♭ + G
④ LH: B♭ + F | RH: A♭ + D + F

Use the exact same rhythm for each.

Once you can do that without stopping, you're ready for the fun part.

④ Play over a real funk drum groove — 8 minutes
I found a 95 BPM funk backing track with drums only.

Funk Drum Groove — 95 BPM, Drums Only (JunzBass Backing Tracks)
Funk Drum Groove — 95 BPM, Drums Only (JunzBass Backing Tracks)
youtube.com
It's just the drums, so there's no bass or keyboard competing with what you're playing.

First 4 minutes: Lock in
Play your three shapes with the rhythm you just learned.

LH: F + C | RH: A♭ + C + E♭
LH: B♭ + F | RH: A♭ + D + F
LH: C + G | RH: B♭ + E♭ + G
LH: B♭ + F | RH: A♭ + D + F

Keep repeating.

Try to get your LH notes lined up with the drumbeat.

Your RH should feel like little rhythmic answers.

Don't speed up when something sounds exciting.

Listen to the drummer, not just yourself.

Next 4 minutes: Make something of your own
Keep the drum track going.

For the first couple of loops, simplify the left hand:

① LH: F | RH: A♭ + C + E♭
② LH: B♭ | RH: A♭ + D + F
③ LH: C | RH: B♭ + E♭ + G
④ LH: B♭ | RH: A♭ + D + F

Then occasionally stop playing the RH chords and use these notes to invent a melody:

C – E♭ – F – G – B♭

Try this simple phrase:

LH: F | RH: C → E♭ → F

Pause.

LH: B♭ | RH: G → F → E♭

Then return to playing the full chords.

Don't try to fill every moment.

If you find a little melody you like, repeat it several times.

That's exactly how a lot of great funk grooves develop: one short, memorable musical idea repeated with slight changes.

⑤ Optional GO:KEYS 3 experiment — 3 minutes
This week, use Split.

Split means assigning a different instrument sound to the lower and upper sections of your keyboard.

We're going for a classic funk combination.

LOWER: Fingered Bass
UPPER: Clav 1

Both are actual Roland GO:KEYS 3 factory tones. Fingered Bass is in the E.Bass category and Clav 1 is in the Clav category. 

A clavinet is an electric keyboard instrument with a short, bright, almost plucked sound. It's particularly associated with 1970s funk.

Set up Split
Press [split/dual] until the screen shows Split.
Select LOWER with [f1] and choose Fingered Bass.
Select UPPER with [f2] and choose Clav 1.
Those controls are documented in Roland's GO:KEYS 3 reference manual. 

Now play the simplified version:

① LH: F | RH: A♭ + C + E♭
② LH: B♭ | RH: A♭ + D + F
③ LH: C | RH: B♭ + E♭ + G
④ LH: B♭ | RH: A♭ + D + F

Keep LH below the keyboard's split point and RH above it.

Use the same rhythm as before.

The sound should immediately become punchier and more like two musicians playing together.

🎧 Apple Music — This week's inspiration
1. Stevie Wonder — Superstition
Listen on Apple Music

Listen specifically to the clavinet.

That incredibly recognizable repeating keyboard part is a fantastic example of funky, rhythmic playing.

Notice how the little notes and chords seem to bounce around the drumbeat.

Also pay attention to how much silence exists between those short keyboard sounds.

You're not learning the song's actual notes today, but you're practicing the same kind of rhythmic coordination.

2. Vulfpeck — Back Pocket
Listen on Apple Music

This is a more modern approach to that funky, laid-back sound.

Listen for the interaction between bass, keyboards, and drums.

Nothing needs to be particularly complicated because every part has its own place.

Notice how the little musical phrases repeat until they become almost hypnotic.

That's exactly what I want you trying to create during your improvisation time.

⭐ What to remember this week
Your entire practice revolves around just three shapes:

① LH: F + C | RH: A♭ + C + E♭
② LH: B♭ + F | RH: A♭ + D + F
③ LH: C + G | RH: B♭ + E♭ + G

Play them in this order: ① → ② → ③ → ②.

The new skill isn't another complicated chord. It's making your playing sound more intentional by shortening notes and leaving rhythmic space.

And when you get to the drum track, resist the urge to keep adding notes.

Find a groove you like. Stay with it. Enjoy how it feels.

originalText:
🎹 Week 9 — Late-Night R&B / Neo-Soul
Warm electric piano, beautiful chords, and a slow, effortless groove
25 minutes | 80 BPM | Roland GO:KEYS 3

This week, we're moving away from last week's punchy funk and into something softer, moodier, and more intimate.

Think Sade, Lauryn Hill, and D'Angelo.

Today's goal: Learn four beautiful chord shapes, discover how smoothly they connect, and play them over a relaxed R&B drumbeat.

We're also introducing a new skill: keeping some right-hand fingers in place while other notes change. This makes your playing sound smoother without requiring more complicated chords.

① Warm-up — 3 minutes
Start around the middle of your keyboard.

We're using five notes:

D♭ – E♭ – F – A♭ – B♭

Four are black keys. F is white.

Play slowly
LH: — | RH: D♭ → E♭ → F → A♭ → B♭

Come back down:

LH: — | RH: B♭ → A♭ → F → E♭ → D♭

Now make two little musical phrases.

LH: — | RH: F → A♭ → B♭

Pause.

LH: — | RH: A♭ → F → E♭ → D♭

Repeat these a few times.

Don't worry about keeping a perfect beat yet.

Listen to how these notes sound together. They're going to become your little melody-making toolkit later.

② Four chords — 6 minutes
These are especially nice because the right-hand shapes move gradually rather than jumping around the keyboard.

Keep your left hand below middle C and your right hand around or above middle C.

① Warm and settled
LH: D♭ + A♭ | RH: F + A♭ + C

② Softer, slightly melancholy
LH: B♭ + F | RH: F + A♭ + D♭

③ A little more tension
LH: E♭ + B♭ | RH: G♭ + B♭ + D♭

④ Floating, wanting to return
LH: A♭ + E♭ | RH: G♭ + C + E♭

Your entire progression
① → ② → ③ → ④ → repeat

For now, play each chord once.

Count:

1 – 2 – 3 – 4

Press both hands on 1.

Hold everything through 2, 3, 4.

Release just before the next 1 and change chords.

Something to notice: When you move from chord ① to chord ②, your RH keeps F and A♭ exactly where they are. Only the top note moves from C to D♭.

That's the sound we're exploring this week: small movements creating beautiful changes.

③ Give it an R&B rhythm — 5 minutes
We're going to play the same four chords, but make them feel less like an exercise and more like an actual keyboard accompaniment.

Count out loud
1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &

Each number is a main beat. Each & is halfway between beats.

Count	1	&	2	&	3	&	4	&
LH	PRESS	HOLD	HOLD	HOLD	HOLD	HOLD	HOLD	RELEASE
RH	PRESS	HOLD	RELEASE	—	—	PRESS	HOLD	RELEASE
Exactly what to do
Start with chord ①.

LH: D♭ + A♭ | RH: F + A♭ + C

1: Press both hands together.

& after 1: Keep holding.

2: Release RH. Keep LH down.

& after 2: Nothing. Let the music breathe.

3: Keep holding LH.

& after 3: Press RH again.

4: Keep holding.

& after 4: Release everything.

On the next 1, move to chord ②.

That's it!

You're playing the right-hand chord twice, but the second hit arrives between the main beats.

This creates a gentle push forward without making the rhythm busy.

Practice this with all four shapes.

🎹 Week 10 — Cinematic Piano
25 minutes · 80 BPM · Roland GO:KEYS 3

This week we're going for something spacious and emotional, like a film soundtrack. Think Ludovico Einaudi or the quiet beginning of a dramatic movie scene.

Last week was about smooth R&B chords. This week we'll build on that by playing the right-hand notes one at a time, letting them rise over a sustained left hand.

Today's goal: Make four simple shapes sound like the beginning of your own soundtrack.

1. Warm up — 3 minutes
Start with a piano sound. Play these notes around the middle of your keyboard.

LH: — | RH: E → G → A → B → D

Then come back down.

LH: — | RH: D → B → A → G → E

Now try a small musical phrase:

LH: — | RH: E → G → B

Pause for two seconds.

LH: — | RH: D → B → G → E

Play this three or four times. Make the last E softer than the first note. Hear how it creates a feeling of coming home.

2. Four shapes — 6 minutes
1
LH: E + B | RH: G + B + E

Dark, thoughtful

2
LH: C + G | RH: G + C + E

Warmer, opening up

3
LH: G + D | RH: G + B + D

Bright, hopeful

4
LH: D + A | RH: F♯ + A + D

Suspended, wanting to return

Play 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → repeat.

For the first few minutes, press all five notes together on count 1, hold through 2, 3, 4, and release just before the next 1.

Notice the right hand hardly has to move between shapes. That's what makes this progression feel connected.

3. Make the notes roll upward — 5 minutes
Now we're going to turn those block chords into a gentle, rising piano pattern.

Instead of pressing all three right-hand notes together, play them one at a time from lowest to highest.

Count slowly: 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &

1

The three highlighted beats are where you press new notes.

For shape 1:

LH: E + B | RH: G → B → E

1: Press LH E + B and RH G.

2: Release RH G and press B.

3: Release RH B and press E.

4: Hold RH E.

Final &: Release everything, ready for the next shape.

Your LH stays down for the entire measure.

Now repeat the same motion for all four shapes:

① LH: E + B | RH: G → B → E

② LH: C + G | RH: G → C → E

③ LH: G + D | RH: G → B → D

④ LH: D + A | RH: F♯ → A → D

This is called a broken chord: the notes that make up a chord are played separately instead of simultaneously.

Play softly at first. Let each rising note feel like it's leading toward something.

4. Play with drums — 8 minutes
Chill Groove Drum Track 80 BPM Guitar Backing Beat #303 - song and lyrics by Guitar Maps Drum Tracks | Spotify
Chill Groove Drum Track — 80 BPM

Guitar Maps Drum Tracks · Drums only

YouTube

E – G – A – B – D

For example:

LH: E + B | RH: B → A → G → E

Then play the normal second shape:

LH: C + G | RH: G → C → E

Don't try to write a whole song. Find one short melody you like and repeat it. Let the drums guide how long you leave between notes.

Try a soft piano layered with a cinematic background sound.

UPPER
Concert Piano — Ac.Piano

LOWER
Soft Warm Pad — Synth Pad/Str

+2

Once that sounds comfortable, try choosing your own note for beat 4. Don't change anything else.

Your quick keyboard cheat sheet
Four shapes. One rhythm.
① LH: C + G | RH: G + C + E

② LH: G + D | RH: G + B + D

③ LH: A + E | RH: A + C + E

LH: Press on 1, hold all the way through 4, release on the final &.

This week's skill is making a repeating chord pattern feel alive. You're combining the held notes from last week's cinematic session with the short rhythmic hits you've practiced in disco and funk. sections.title: Chord shapes — 6 minutes
sections.instructions:
1. LH: C + G | RH: G + C + E
2. LH: G + D | RH: G + B + D
3. LH: A + E | RH: A + C + E
4. LH: F + C | RH: A + C + F

Play 1 → 2 → 3 → 4, then repeat.

Initially, press both hands together on beat 1, hold through beat 4, and release just before the next beat 1.

sections.title: Rhythm — 5 minutes
sections.instructions:
Count: 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &

For each chord:
1: Press LH and RH together.
First &: Release RH while holding LH.
2: Continue holding LH.
& after 2: Press RH chord again.
3: Release RH.
& after 3: Continue holding LH.
4: Press RH chord again.
Final &: Release everything.

Repeat the same rhythm for the next chord.
